qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Define government economic policy.
items.canonical_answer: Government decisions and actions intended to influence economic activity towards specified aims.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): government action influencing activity towards aims.
objective_titles: Define government economic policy

items.prompt: Identify an aim and an instrument in an invented policy using a tax reduction to support employment.
items.canonical_answer: Higher employment is the aim; the tax reduction is the instrument.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): employment aim. Distinction/characteristic (1): tax instrument.
objective_titles: Define government economic policy

items.prompt: Evaluate a proposed spending expansion where workers and equipment are idle but some materials must be imported and the stated budget has limited financing capacity.
items.canonical_answer: Spending can create demand and use idle resources, supporting output and jobs. Imports can absorb some demand and add external payments, while limited finance constrains the size. A targeted affordable expansion is more defensible than an unlimited one if suppliers can respond; price and external stability must still be monitored.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): demand rises (1), idle resources can produce (1). Argument against (2): imports/external pressure (1), funding limit (1). Condition (1): affordable targeted spending and responsive suppliers. Judgement (2): limited expansion supported (1), tied to employment versus stability trade-off (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss the aims of government policy and why they should be achieved - full employment - prevention of inflation - economic growth - redistribution of income - balance of payments stability

items.prompt: Explain the error in using population growth alone as evidence of economic growth.
items.canonical_answer: Population growth increases the number of people; economic growth increases real output. Output per person may fall if population rises faster than real production.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): people count mistaken for output. Boundary/test (1): compare real output and population separately.
objective_titles: Discuss the aims of government policy and why they should be achieved - full employment - prevention of inflation - economic growth - redistribution of income - balance of payments stability

items.prompt: Explain why hiring genuinely unemployed suitable workers for useful maintenance can support the employment aim when funding and spare equipment are available.
items.canonical_answer: The programme creates demand for previously idle labour. Workers earn income and use spare equipment to produce useful services, increasing employment and output under the stated conditions.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the stated policy or economic condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two causal links. Consequence (1): effect on the stated aim or activity, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain full employment through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why filling a programme entirely by recruiting workers already employed elsewhere does not establish the same net employment gain as hiring unemployed workers.
items.canonical_answer: Hiring may shift existing employment rather than create an equal net increase. The source of recruits matters when judging the economy-wide employment effect.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the supplied policy or household/business facts. Reason/conclusion (1): explain the consequence under the stated conditions.
objective_titles: Explain full employment through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why restraining demand can limit inflationary pressure when spending is rising faster than firms can expand output.
items.canonical_answer: Restraint reduces growth in orders and purchasing pressure. With limited capacity, less competition for available output can slow general price increases, although activity may also weaken.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the stated policy or economic condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two causal links. Consequence (1): effect on the stated aim or activity, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain prevention of inflation through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain the price-level implication when inflation falls from 10% to 5% while remaining positive.
items.canonical_answer: Prices continue rising but more slowly. Lower inflation is not the same as a falling general price level.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the supplied policy or household/business facts. Reason/conclusion (1): explain the consequence under the stated conditions.
objective_titles: Explain prevention of inflation through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain how useful infrastructure can support real growth where unreliable transport currently limits saleable production and the project is funded and maintained.
items.canonical_answer: Improved transport reduces disruption and enables resources to reach production and markets. Firms can produce more real output when this removes the bottleneck; living-standard gains still depend on per-capita output, distribution and environmental costs.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the stated policy or economic condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two causal links. Consequence (1): effect on the stated aim or activity, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain economic growth through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why real output growth of 4% with population growth of 6% does not establish higher average living standards.
items.canonical_answer: Population rises faster than output, so output per person falls. Distribution, environmental conditions and other welfare factors also matter; a larger total alone is insufficient.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the supplied policy or household/business facts. Reason/conclusion (1): explain the consequence under the stated conditions.
objective_titles: Explain economic growth through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain the cash redistribution effect when a low-income household pays N$100 extra tax but receives a N$300 support payment, with other conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Tax reduces resources N$100 and the transfer raises them N$300. The net N$200 increase can support essential spending; examining both flows establishes the household’s gain.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the stated policy or economic condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two causal links. Consequence (1): effect on the stated aim or activity, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain redistribution of income through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why a progressive tax label alone does not prove that an entire budget benefits poorer households most.
items.canonical_answer: The spending and benefits financed may go to other groups. Net redistribution depends on both taxes paid and benefits received, not the tax-rate pattern alone.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the supplied policy or household/business facts. Reason/conclusion (1): explain the consequence under the stated conditions.
objective_titles: Explain redistribution of income through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why a domestic spending expansion can increase external pressure when much of the additional purchasing is imported and external financing is limited.
items.canonical_answer: Higher purchases raise import payments rather than only domestic output. Greater external outflows need financing, so limited financing makes the external position harder to sustain; the import content conditions the effect.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the stated policy or economic condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two causal links. Consequence (1): effect on the stated aim or activity, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain balance of payments stability through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why a zero goods trade balance is not a complete test of balance of payments stability.
items.canonical_answer: The external accounts also include other transactions and financing. Equal goods exports and imports alone do not establish sustainability of the full external position.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the supplied policy or household/business facts. Reason/conclusion (1): explain the consequence under the stated conditions.
objective_titles: Explain balance of payments stability through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Identify the policy categories for an income-tax change and a central-bank interest-rate action.
items.canonical_answer: The income-tax change is fiscal; the interest-rate action is monetary.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): tax fiscal. Distinction/example (1): interest monetary.
objective_titles: Explain fiscal and monetary policies of the government

items.prompt: Explain the confusion in calling an income-tax reduction monetary policy because it can increase spending.
items.canonical_answer: It is fiscal policy because the instrument changes taxation. Monetary policy acts through money, credit or interest conditions; a shared spending effect does not erase the instrument boundary.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): outcome used to misclassify instrument. Boundary/test (1): taxation fiscal versus credit/interest monetary.
objective_titles: Explain fiscal and monetary policies of the government

items.prompt: Explain how public purchases can support activity when domestic firms have spare capacity, suitable workers are unemployed and the spending is funded.
items.canonical_answer: Orders increase demand for output. Firms can use idle capacity and hire suitable workers to fulfil them, supporting output and employment; the resource and funding conditions make the response feasible.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the stated policy or economic condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two causal links. Consequence (1): effect on the stated aim or activity, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain fiscal policy through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why a tax cut does not guarantee an equal increase in domestic spending.
items.canonical_answer: Recipients may save, repay debt or buy imports. Only the part spent on domestic output directly raises that demand through this channel.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the supplied policy or household/business facts. Reason/conclusion (1): explain the consequence under the stated conditions.
objective_titles: Explain fiscal policy through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain how higher lending rates can restrain credit-financed spending when lenders pass through the change and borrowers respond. Use a generic transmission example rather than an unrestricted Namibia rate choice.
items.canonical_answer: Higher interest raises repayment costs, making some purchases or projects less attractive. Postponement reduces demand and can restrain demand-related price pressure. Actual Namibia choices must support the maintained rand peg.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the stated policy or economic condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two causal links. Consequence (1): effect on the stated aim or activity, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain monetary policy through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why a firm with very weak expected sales may not invest after a lending-rate reduction; actual Namibia decisions remain constrained by the rand peg.
items.canonical_answer: Cheaper credit lowers financing cost but does not create enough expected buyers. A project may remain unattractive, so the interest incentive need not overcome weak demand.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the supplied policy or household/business facts. Reason/conclusion (1): explain the consequence under the stated conditions.
objective_titles: Explain monetary policy through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain the distinction between direct/indirect and progressive/proportional classifications of taxation.
items.canonical_answer: Direct/indirect concern the tax base, such as income versus expenditure. Progressive/proportional concern how the average rate changes with income or the relevant base.
marking_guidance: Difference (1): base classification. Contrast/test (1): burden pattern classification.
objective_titles: Describe the different types of taxes

items.prompt: Explain the rate pattern in invented income liabilities of N$200 on N$2,000 and N$600 on N$6,000.
items.canonical_answer: Both are 10% of income, so the tax is proportional across these points. A larger cash payment does not show a higher average rate.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the supplied policy or household/business facts. Reason/conclusion (1): explain the consequence under the stated conditions.
objective_titles: Describe the different types of taxes

items.prompt: Explain the error in describing an identical N$200 payment on incomes N$2,000 and N$6,000 as a proportional income tax.
items.canonical_answer: The shares are 10% and about 3.33%, so the average burden falls. Proportional means equal percentage, not equal cash.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): equal cash mistaken for equal rate. Boundary/test (1): compare 10% with 3.33%.
objective_titles: Describe the different types of taxes

items.prompt: Define direct tax.
items.canonical_answer: A tax imposed directly on income, profit or wealth.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): A tax imposed directly on income, profit or wealth.
objective_titles: Describe direct taxes

items.prompt: Identify the bases making an invented earnings tax and profits tax direct taxes.
items.canonical_answer: The bases are personal income and business profit.
marking_guidance: Feature/characteristic (1): first requested base, rate or liability. Distinction/example (1): second requested feature or correctly evidenced category.
objective_titles: Describe direct taxes

items.prompt: Define indirect tax.
items.canonical_answer: A tax imposed on expenditure or transactions involving goods and services.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): A tax imposed on expenditure or transactions involving goods and services.
objective_titles: Describe indirect taxes

items.prompt: Identify the taxable transaction and category in an invented N$2 charge on each soap bar sold.
items.canonical_answer: The sale of the bar is the taxed transaction; the charge is an indirect tax.
marking_guidance: Feature/characteristic (1): first requested base, rate or liability. Distinction/example (1): second requested feature or correctly evidenced category.
objective_titles: Describe indirect taxes

items.prompt: Define progressive taxation.
items.canonical_answer: Taxation whose average rate rises as income or the relevant taxable base rises.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Taxation whose average rate rises as income or the relevant taxable base rises.
objective_titles: Describe progressive taxation

items.prompt: Identify the average rates and pattern for invented tax N$100 on N$2,000 income and N$600 on N$6,000.
items.canonical_answer: Rates rise from 5% to 10%, a progressive pattern.
marking_guidance: Feature/characteristic (1): first requested base, rate or liability. Distinction/example (1): second requested feature or correctly evidenced category.
objective_titles: Describe progressive taxation

items.prompt: Define proportional taxation.
items.canonical_answer: Taxation whose average rate stays constant as the taxable base rises.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Taxation whose average rate stays constant as the taxable base rises.
objective_titles: Describe proportional taxation

items.prompt: Identify the cash liabilities on N$2,000 and N$6,000 under an invented proportional 10% income tax.
items.canonical_answer: The liabilities are N$200 and N$600, each 10%.
marking_guidance: Feature/characteristic (1): first requested base, rate or liability. Distinction/example (1): second requested feature or correctly evidenced category.
objective_titles: Describe proportional taxation

items.prompt: Define regressive taxation.
items.canonical_answer: Taxation whose average burden falls as an income share as income rises.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Taxation whose average burden falls as an income share as income rises.
objective_titles: Describe regressive taxation

items.prompt: Identify the burden pattern for an invented equal N$100 levy on incomes N$1,000 and N$5,000. Include the two shares.
items.canonical_answer: The shares are 10% and 2%, giving a regressive pattern.
marking_guidance: Feature/characteristic (1): first requested base, rate or liability. Distinction/example (1): second requested feature or correctly evidenced category.
objective_titles: Describe regressive taxation

items.prompt: Evaluate a tax-funded public equipment project where suitable unemployed workers and spare domestic capacity are available, the equipment removes a documented production bottleneck, but tax reduces some private purchasing power and implementation takes time.
items.canonical_answer: The project can demand output now and improve productive capacity once useful equipment operates. The tax withdraws private purchasing power and delays reduce immediate benefit. Support depends on benefits from the bottleneck repair outweighing these costs, affordable delivery and actual use; no net output gain is established solely by equal tax and spending totals.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): idle resources can respond (1), productive bottleneck eased (1). Argument against (2): private spending withdrawal (1), implementation delay (1). Condition (1): useful affordable delivery and net benefits. Judgement (2): conditional support (1), linked to supplied capacity rather than an automatic net gain (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss how taxes are used by the government to influence business activities and the role of the budget

items.prompt: Explain the error in calling government expenditure above revenue a trade deficit.
items.canonical_answer: That is a government budget deficit. A trade deficit compares imports with exports, so it uses different flows and can coexist with a different budget balance.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): budget versus trade account. Boundary/test (1): revenue/expenditure versus exports/imports.
objective_titles: Discuss how taxes are used by the government to influence business activities and the role of the budget

items.prompt: Explain why depositing savings in a bank is not by itself proof of economic investment in new productive capital.
items.canonical_answer: The deposit is saving or a financial transaction. New productive investment requires equipment, infrastructure or other productive capital to be created or acquired; any later lending towards it is a separate event.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): savings deposit equated with capital formation. Boundary/test (1): require actual productive-capital creation/acquisition.
objective_titles: Discuss how taxes are used by the government to influence business activities and the role of the budget

items.prompt: Explain the business effect of an illustrative lending-rate rise from 8% to 10% on a N$100,000 one-year simple-interest loan, no fees, unchanged expected receipts. Actual Namibia policy must support the rand peg.
items.canonical_answer: Interest rises N$8,000 to N$10,000, adding N$2,000 cost. This reduces the project’s expected net gain and may postpone a borderline investment; the decision depends on expected returns and credit conditions.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): identify the stated policy or economic condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two causal links. Consequence (1): effect on the stated aim or activity, with its condition.
objective_titles: Describe how the government can use the interest rate to influence business activity

items.prompt: Explain why an unborrowed business can still be affected by higher lending rates when its customers rely on credit; actual Namibia policy remains within the rand-peg framework.
items.canonical_answer: Customers may postpone financed purchases as repayment costs rise. Lower orders can reduce the business’s activity even without its own borrowing.
marking_guidance: Context (1): use the supplied policy or household/business facts. Reason/conclusion (1): explain the consequence under the stated conditions.
objective_titles: Describe how the government can use the interest rate to influence business activity

items.prompt: Define government economic policy (2). Identify two policy aims (2). Explain a fiscal transmission step where a tax cut leaves households more disposable income and they spend part on domestic output with spare capacity (2). Identify the categories of an invented income tax and a tax on product sales (2).
items.canonical_answer: Policy is government decisions/actions influencing activity towards aims. Employment and price stability are aims. The tax cut can raise domestic demand and output under the stated spending/capacity conditions. Income tax is direct; product-sales tax indirect.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): government actions (1), economic activity towards aims (1). Separate points for aims (2): employment (1), price stability (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented Namibia policy case under the maintained one-to-one Namibia dollar/rand peg. Suitable workers are unemployed and some domestic equipment is idle, while input prices are rising because imported materials are scarce. External financing is limited. A tax-funded public equipment programme addresses a documented transport bottleneck, but the tax reduces some household disposable income and delivery takes time. A separate illustrative lending-rate increase would be passed to new loans and raise credit costs. These are teaching conditions, not current policy announcements. Describe three policy aims relevant to the case, each with a case detail (6). Explain the different fiscal and interest-rate channels affecting activity, respecting the currency framework (7). Discuss the tax-funded programme’s merits and limitations for business activity and the budget (7).
items.canonical_answer: Employment uses idle labour; price stability addresses rising costs; external stability matters with limited financing. Fiscal equipment spending orders output, while tax can reduce private spending. Higher new-loan rates raise borrowing costs and may delay private projects or customer purchases. Namibia decisions must support the rand peg; interest restraint does not directly create scarce imports. The useful programme can improve capacity but tax withdrawal, delays and import needs limit its immediate effect. Conditional support depends on affordable implementation and bottleneck benefits exceeding costs.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): employment aim (1), unemployed workers detail (1); price stability (1), rising input prices detail (1); external stability (1), limited financing detail (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): government orders output (1), tax withdraws disposable funds (1); rates raise new-loan cost (1), some projects postponed (1), credit-financed customer demand weakens (1); demand effect differs from direct import supply (1), peg constraint retained (1). Both sides/judgement (7): programme removes bottleneck (1), idle domestic resources can respond (1); tax withdrawal (1), delays/import costs (1); condition funded useful delivery (1); judgement conditional support (1), tied to net budget/business effects (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Invented Namibia cases under the maintained rand peg. Case 1: tax-funded public equipment addresses a transport bottleneck during unemployment; domestic capacity is spare, funding is affordable, but taxes reduce some private disposable income and delivery takes time. Case 2: output capacity is tight, general price pressure is strong, imported inputs are scarce and external financing is limited; a similar broad spending expansion is proposed. Interest-rate decisions must support the peg, with no unrestricted independent rate choice assumed. Evaluate the tax-funded investment in Case 1 against employment and growth aims (7). Evaluate a broad budget expansion in Case 2 against growth, inflation and external-stability aims (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: orders can employ idle resources and usable equipment can expand productive capacity, but tax withdrawal and delay offset some benefits. Support depends on efficient delivery and useful net gains, with distribution, per-capita output and environmental effects relevant to living standards. Case 2: expansion may support some activity but tight capacity, imported scarcity and limited financing increase price/external risks. Prefer a targeted feasible response over broad expansion under these conditions, retaining the rand-peg constraint on monetary options.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for jobs (1), capacity growth (1); argument against tax withdrawal (1), delay (1); condition useful affordable delivery (1); judgement conditional support (1), tied to spare resources/net gains (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for activity (1), possible targeted capacity repair (1); argument against inflation pressure (1), imports/financing constraint (1); condition tight capacity and peg respected (1); judgement broad expansion weakly supported (1), favour feasible targeting tied to conditions (1). Total 14.
